docs.text:
• Publishing Agents and Skills: configure the sources these checks run against.
  • Jev assessment: the optional AI assessment that runs on each Version.
  • Scanning configuration: Trivy and scan policy settings.

docs.title: Verify with Agent Hooks
docs.text:
opendepot verify checks that every installed skill and agent still matches the hash recorded in opendepot.lock.hcl. On its own, it runs only when you run it. A tool hook runs it before each tool call an agent makes. When a check fails, the hook does not stop the agent. It tells the agent how to restore the item with opendepot apply, and it allows that restore to run.

The hook is the enforcement layer. The CLI does not block edits by itself.

docs.title: Signatures and hashes
docs.text:
The version controller signs the SHA256SUMS file for each skill and agent version with a GPG (OpenPGP) key. The server serves the detached signature at SHA256SUMS.sig. The signature shows who published the version. It does not encrypt the content.

The checks happen in two places:

  1. At install. apply verifies the SHA256SUMS signature against the signing key pinned on first use. It also checks that the archive matches the signed hash, then records the installed file hashes in opendepot.lock.hcl.
  2. At each tool call. The hook runs verify, which hashes the installed files and compares them with the lock file. It does not check the signature again, and it makes no network calls.

So verify catches edits to installed files after install. It trusts the lock file, so review changes to opendepot.lock.hcl in the same way as opendepot.hcl. Set signing_key in opendepot.hcl to pin the expected signer. A signer change then fails the install instead of prompting.

docs.title: How the hook responds
docs.text:
1. Before each tool call, the hook runs opendepot verify. If it passes, the call runs.
  2. If it fails, the hook blocks the call and gives the agent the reason: do not edit installed files, run opendepot apply, then retry.
  3. The hook lets through only the exact commands opendepot apply and opendepot verify. Calls such as opendepot apply --force, chained commands, and reads of the installed file stay blocked.
  4. The agent runs opendepot apply, which rewrites the installed files from the lock file. The retried call passes.

If apply refuses because someone edited an AGENTS.md block by hand, the agent stops and tells you. The hook does not allow --force, which would overwrite that edit.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The current write is not blocked. A hook runs before a tool call, so an edit the agent makes with its current call still lands on disk. The next tool call fails verification, and the agent restores the file.
  • Hook config is editable by the agent. .claude/settings.json, .codex/hooks.json, and .github/hooks/*.json live in the repository. An agent could remove the hook. Use managed hooks where you need to prevent this. See Managed hooks.
  • Config changes are not guarded. The agent can edit opendepot.hcl and run apply to install a different version. The hook checks installed files, not the config. Commit opendepot.hcl and opendepot.lock.hcl so changes show up in review.
  • Run hooks only in repositories with a lock file. verify fails without opendepot.lock.hcl, so a hook in a repository without one blocks every tool call. Add hook config to projects that use opendepot apply. Do not add it to your user-level settings, which apply to every project.
  • Run the agent from the project root. The hook reads opendepot.lock.hcl from the directory the agent runs in.
  • Copilot checks once per batch of tool calls. If the agent issues an edit and a read in the same batch, the read runs without a check. The next batch is checked.
  • Codex hooks must be reviewed before they run. An unreviewed hook is skipped without a warning. See Codex.
  • The hooks feature can be turned off. Codex has a [features] hooks = false setting. Use managed requirements if you rely on this control.

Claude Code and Codex receive the hook's stderr message as the tool result. Copilot does not show a non-zero exit's stderr to the model, so its hook writes a JSON deny with the reason to stdout instead.

Copilot was tested with a real model, gpt-6-luna. Claude Code 2.1.311 and Codex 0.169.0 were tested with a scripted model, which checks the hook contract but not how a model acts. The restore command for those two was tested offline with sample payloads. It has not been run in a real Claude Code or Codex session.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
Add this to .claude/settings.json in the project root. The "*" matcher runs the hook for every tool, including tools in subagents.

{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "*",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "input=$(cat); opendepot verify >/dev/null 2>&1 && exit 0; printf '%s' \"$input\" | grep -Eq '\"command\"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*\"opendepot (apply|verify)\"([[:space:],}]|$)' && exit 0; echo 'OpenDepot: an installed skill or agent changed. Do not edit installed files. Run opendepot apply to restore it from the lock file, then retry. If apply refuses because an AGENTS.md block was edited by hand, stop and tell the user.' >&2; exit 2"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

Claude Code merges hook settings across user, project, and managed levels. A hook in your user settings runs in every project, so keep this one in the project file. See Managed hooks for restricting hooks to managed ones.

docs.title: Codex
docs.text:
Add this to .codex/hooks.json in the project root. The ".*" matcher covers every tool that PreToolUse fires for.

{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": ".*",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "input=$(cat); opendepot verify >/dev/null 2>&1 && exit 0; printf '%s' \"$input\" | grep -Eq '\"command\"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*\"opendepot (apply|verify)\"([[:space:],}]|$)' && exit 0; echo 'OpenDepot: an installed skill or agent changed. Do not edit installed files. Run opendepot apply to restore it from the lock file, then retry. If apply refuses because an AGENTS.md block was edited by hand, stop and tell the user.' >&2; exit 2",
            "timeout": 30
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

Codex runs a hook only after you review it. The interactive CLI prompts for review before an unreviewed hook runs. In testing, an unreviewed hook did not run, and a tampered skill was read with no warning. codex exec --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust skips the review. Use it only for testing. This page does not cover a headless setup that trusts hooks through config.

docs.title: Copilot
docs.text:
Add this to .github/hooks/opendepot.json. Copilot's preToolUse event fires for every tool, so it has no matcher.

{
  "version": 1,
  "hooks": {
    "preToolUse": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "bash": "input=$(cat); opendepot verify >/dev/null 2>&1 && exit 0; printf '%s' \"$input\" | grep -Eq '\"command\"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*\"opendepot (apply|verify)\"([[:space:],}]|$)' && exit 0; printf '%s\\n' '{\"permissionDecision\": \"deny\", \"permissionDecisionReason\": \"OpenDepot: an installed skill or agent changed. Do not edit installed files. Run opendepot apply to restore it from the lock file, then retry. If apply refuses because an AGENTS.md block was edited by hand, stop and tell the user.\"}'",
        "timeoutSec": 60
      }
    ]
  }
}

The hook reads the tool call from stdin and checks toolArgs.command. When the check fails, it prints a JSON permissionDecision: deny with the reason and exits 0. A non-zero exit also blocks the call, but the agent receives only hook exited with code 2. The Windows PowerShell form is not covered here because it has not been tested.

Copilot loads project hooks only when the folder is trusted. Add the project path to trustedFolders in your Copilot config (~/.copilot/config.json). In testing, an untrusted project's hook did not run.

docs.title: Example run
docs.text:
These runs used Copilot CLI 1.0.112 and the small model gpt-6-luna. The installed skill was opendepot-system/gh-actions-debug 0.9.0 from demo.opendepot.defdev.io, and the hook above was in .github/hooks/opendepot.json. Each run passed --add-dir for the skill folder, which sits outside the project. Without it, Copilot's own permission check denies the read before the hook runs. The stats footer is removed.

The clean state, where the skill matches the lock file:

 MD Read ~/.copilot/skills/gh-actions-debug/SKILL.md L1:1 (1 line read)

---

The tampered state, after a line was appended to the skill and the agent was asked to read it:

 MD Read ~/.copilot/skills/gh-actions-debug/SKILL.md Denied by preToolUse hook: OpenDepot: an insta…
   Denied by preToolUse hook: OpenDepot: an installed skill or agent changed. Do not edit installed
   files. Run opendepot apply to restore it from the lock file, then retry. If apply refuses because
   an AGENTS.md block was edited by hand, stop and tell the user.

 ✗ skill(gh-actions-debug)
   Denied by preToolUse hook: OpenDepot: an installed skill or agent changed. Do not edit installed
   files. Run opendepot apply to restore it from the lock file, then retry. If apply refuses because
   an AGENTS.md block was edited by hand, stop and tell the user.

 $ Shell Restore locked skill installation 14 lines…
   opendepot apply

 MD Read ~/.copilot/skills/gh-actions-debug/SKILL.md L1:1 (1 line read)

---

The agent first tried to load the skill with the skill tool and then to read the file. The hook denied both. The agent then ran opendepot apply, which the hook allowed. Its retried read passed, and the file matched the locked version afterward.

The session log records each hook decision. This excerpt is trimmed to the fields that matter:

hook.start   preToolUse  view  SKILL.md
hook.end     success: true   output: "Denied by preToolUse hook: OpenDepot: ..."
tool.execution_complete  view   success: false
hook.start   preToolUse  skill  gh-actions-debug
hook.end     success: true   output: "Denied by preToolUse hook: OpenDepot: ..."
tool.execution_complete  skill  success: false
hook.start   preToolUse  bash  opendepot apply
hook.end     success: true   output: ""
tool.execution_complete  bash   success: true
hook.start   preToolUse  view  SKILL.md
hook.end     success: true   output: ""
tool.execution_complete  view   success: true

success: true on hook.end means the hook ran. The denial is in its output.

docs.title: Unattended runs
docs.text:
The restore does not need a person. The agent runs opendepot apply itself, so a run with nobody watching still recovers from a changed skill or agent. The restore installs the version in opendepot.lock.hcl. It does not upgrade.

Two cases still need a person:

  • A hand-edited AGENTS.md block. Plain apply refuses it, and the hook blocks apply --force. The agent stops and reports the block. Decide whether to keep the edit, then run apply --force yourself if you want to overwrite it.
  • A failed restore. If the registry is unreachable or the credentials are missing, apply fails, the hook keeps blocking, and the agent reports the failure. The agent's environment needs the same registry access and credentials that apply uses.

On the demo registry, apply took a median of about 1.2 s over three runs (1.15–1.5 s). It runs only after a failed check, so a passing check still costs the usual few milliseconds.

docs.title: Optional: automatic apply --force
docs.text:
If nobody can answer the agent's stop-and-report, you can add a second hook that runs opendepot apply --force when verify fails. Use it only if you accept that it overwrites hand edits in AGENTS.md blocks without asking.

The skill and agent restore does not need --force. Plain apply already restores them, so --force only changes the case where an AGENTS.md block was edited by hand. Leave this hook out unless that trade-off is acceptable.

docs.title: Latency
docs.text:
The check is local. It reads the lock file, hashes the installed files, and compares them, with no network calls. Each tool call pays that cost once. Measured on macOS, with the verify command the hook runs:

Installed content opendepot verify in the hook (median) 1 skill, 8 KB about 10 ms 25 skills, 600 KB about 14–17 ms 10 skills × 200 files, about 8 MB about 45 ms

The clean and tampered paths do the same check, so their times match. The shell itself adds about 3 ms. In a Copilot run on the 25-skill project, the five hook invocations each took 16–20 ms, as recorded in the session log. Cost grows with the number of installed bytes, not with the number of tool calls.

docs.title: Managed hooks
docs.text:
A project hook can be removed by the agent that it guards. To prevent that, deploy the hook from an administrator-controlled location and tell each harness to use only those hooks.

  • Claude Code: set allowManagedHooksOnly in managed settings. Only hooks from managed settings run.
  • Codex: set allow_managed_hooks_only = true in requirements.toml, and point [hooks] managed_dir at the directory that holds the hook config.
  • Copilot: Copilot also supports administrator-deployed hooks. See GitHub's hooks reference for how to deploy them.

The managed settings above come from each vendor's documentation. They were not tested here. Check each harness's documentation for the exact file locations on your platform before you rely on managed hooks.

docs.title: Jev Digest, Exemptions, and Retries
docs.text: Read the Jev digest for a Version, clear a Jev block with an exemption, and understand how failed Jev calls are retried. For how Jev is enabled and scored, see Jev assessment.

docs.title: Reading the digest
docs.text:
Each fresh Jev assessment records the SHA-256 of the archive it assessed in status.jevAssessment.contentDigest. A jevExemptions entry uses this value. Read it with kubectl:

kubectl get version <version-name> \
  --namespace opendepot-system \
  --output jsonpath='{.status.jevAssessment.contentDigest}'

The Jev panel shows the same digest with a copy button.

status.checksum holds the same SHA-256 bytes as base64. contentDigest holds them as lowercase hex. To convert status.checksum:

kubectl get version <version-name> \
  --namespace opendepot-system \
  --output jsonpath='{.status.checksum}' | base64 --decode | xxd -p -c 64

A legacy assessment, recorded before contentDigest existed, has no digest, so no exemption can match it. Set forceSync: true on the Version once, as on line 282. The new assessment records the digest.

docs.title: Exemptions
docs.text:
A ScanPolicy clears a Jev block with a jevExemptions entry. Each entry matches one exact archive digest. For the fields, see Jev exemptions with ScanPolicy.

What an exemption clears. A matching entry clears every Jev block reason for the exact digest. That covers the verdict reasons (Critical, each of the eight thresholds, and minConfidence) and the coverage reasons: skipped files, the token limit, content that needs more than 16 parts, a failed part, retries that are exhausted, an unreadable token Secret, a read error on the extracted content, and Jev disabled on the controller. An exemption does not change needsReview. The Workshop Needs review queue and the Stats Needs review count leave out a Version while its exemption is active, so a Version that is still flagged shows up again once exemptionExpires passes. An exemption with no expiry stays out of the queue until it is removed.

When the Jev call failed. If the assessment ends with a Service error, the exemption is still recorded. exempted is true and blocked is false. The Version still stays unsynced with status.synced: false and a JevUnavailable: sync status. It publishes only after a Jev run completes without an error. When retries are exhausted, the Version stays unsynced until you set forceSync: true or change the spec. Check status.synced and syncStatus before you treat a Version as published.

Entries are not tied to the reasons they were granted for. An entry clears whatever reasons the assessment has while the digest matches. If you tighten jevPolicy and then force a sync, the same entry also clears the new reasons, as long as the archive digest is unchanged.

The digest depends on the toolchain and the packing code. Archives are packed with a deterministic tar and gzip writer that uses the Go compress/flate implementation. A Go toolchain upgrade, or a change to how archives are packed, produces a new digest. The old entry no longer matches, so the Version blocks again. Add an entry for the new digest after you review the assessment.

Audit. Use these to see which entries apply:

  • status.jevAssessment fields: exempted, exemptedBy, exemptionReason, exemptionExpires, blockReasons, and blocked.
  • syncStatus on a published exempted Version names the policy, the number of cleared reasons, the first 12 characters of the digest, and the expiry.
  • Events: JevExemptionApplied (Normal) when an entry starts to apply, and JevExemptionRevoked (Warning) when it stops. Events are emitted on a change only. The revoked message does not say why the entry stopped applying, so check the policy's expires and its exemption list. Run kubectl describe version <version-name> to view them. JevExemptionApplied also appears when the Jev call failed and the Version stays unsynced.
  • ScanPolicy status.activeJevExemptions and status.expiredJevExemptions count the entries.

Branch sources. A Rejected branch Version that has no assigned version is re-opened when the winning ScanPolicy has an unexpired jevExemptions entry for its stored digest. The controller downloads the archive again. It checks the digest against the entry after the download, so only the exact archive publishes.

docs.title: Retries
docs.text:
A Service failure is retried every 15 seconds. The controller counts each failure in controller memory, keyed by the Version, its generation, and its archive checksum, and copies the count to status.jevAssessment.retryCount. The count does not depend on the status write, so retries stop even when the API server rejects that write. Retries stop once the count exceeds jevMaxRetries. With the default of 3, a Version gets 4 attempts. After that, the error stays recorded until you set forceSync: true or change the spec. Either one bumps the generation and starts a new count. A controller restart also clears the in-memory count, and the next run starts again from the stored retryCount. Each attempt makes at most 16 Jev requests.

A 401 or 403 from Jev is retried every 15 seconds and is not counted. These retries continue until the token is fixed.

Set scanning.jev.maxRetries to change the limit. It maps to the --jev-max-retries flag on the version controller.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Jev assessment: enable Jev and review how Versions are scored.
  • Scanning configuration: ScanPolicy fields, including jevExemptions.

docs.title: Jev Assessment
docs.text: Jev is the TypeSafe AI assessment. It is optional and off by default. The chart sets scanning.jev.enabled: false. When it is enabled, the version controller asks Jev a fixed set of questions about each Skill or Agent Version and records the answers in status.jevAssessment. Jev can block a Version. It never bypasses signature or hash checks. The CLI still verifies the SHA256SUMS signature and the hashes before it installs anything.

docs.title: Enabling Jev
docs.text:
1. Enable Jev on the version controller:

    helm upgrade opendepot chart/opendepot \
  --set scanning.jev.enabled=true

    The scanning.jev.endpoint value defaults to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. Override it only if TypeSafe gives you a different endpoint. The endpoint must use https://. Plain http:// is accepted only for loopback addresses (localhost, 127.0.0.1, or ::1), which is useful for local development.

    The scanning.jev.maxRetries value sets how many times a failed assessment is retried. It defaults to 3. See Retries.

  2. Create a Secret in the Depot namespace that holds your Jev token under the jevToken key. Use kubectl create secret so the token does not appear in shell history or in a manifest:

    kubectl create secret generic jev-token \
  --namespace opendepot-system \
  --from-file=jevToken=./jev-token.txt

  3. Reference the Secret and a policy from the source. jevSecretRef supplies the Secret name, and the key defaults to jevToken when omitted:

    agentConfigs:
  - name: code-reviewer
    repoOwner: my-org
    repoUrl: https://github.com/my-org/code-reviewer-agent
    jevSecretRef:
      name: jev-token
    jevPolicy:
      maxInjectionProbability: 0.5
      maxExfiltrationProbability: 0.5
      minConfidence: 0.7

docs.title: Questions asked
docs.text:
Each Version is assessed with these questions. The skill or agent word is filled in from the Version type.

Question Answer used Is this skill or agent safe to use? safeProbability Is this skill or agent susceptible to prompt injection, or does it contain text that targets an AI reviewer, scanner, or evaluator? injectionProbability Does it read, collect, or send data, files, environment variables, or credentials to an external destination, including through bundled scripts or code? exfiltrationProbability Does it direct the agent to take destructive or irreversible actions without asking the user first? destructiveProbability Does it contain hidden or obfuscated instructions or code, such as encoded text, compiled or binary artifacts, or instructions to conceal actions? hiddenInstructionsProbability Does it ask the agent to do things beyond what its description says? scopeMismatchProbability Does it direct the agent to download and run remote code or scripts, install unpinned dependencies, or redirect package registries, shell profiles, or git config to untrusted sources? remoteExecutionProbability How much harm could it cause if an AI agent follows its instructions or a user runs its bundled scripts? riskScore, riskLevel, and riskConfidence

Each yes-or-no question also has a definition of what counts as a yes, which keeps the answers consistent across Versions. The yes-or-no questions ask Jev to judge the worst behavior anywhere in the content, even when a part contains only a fragment of a larger file. The risk question asks for the same thing, so a single harmful section can raise the score for the whole Version.

docs.title: How content is split
docs.text:
Jev assesses a Version in parts. Each part is one request, and a Version has at most 16 parts. Content that needs more parts is blocked before any Jev call is made.

  • Order. Part 1 holds the entry file, then the bundled file list. Other files follow in list order. When the list does not fit in part 1, it continues in a later part under Bundled files (continued):.
  • File boundaries. A part ends at a file boundary when it can. A file that does not fit in the rest of its part is split across parts. Each segment has a header such as [part 1 of 2, bytes 0-43999 of 90000], and a segment that continues ends with [continues in part 2].
  • Halving. When Jev rejects a part with max_tokens_exceeded, the part is halved at its midpoint and both halves are sent. The halves take a suffix, such as 3a and 3b. A part can be halved twice, so a half can split again into labels such as 3aa and 3ab. Both halves keep the index of the original part.
  • Evidence view. When a Version has more than one part, one more request is sent. It holds excerpts, with file names and line numbers, of the lines that match a signal group: exfiltration destinations, outbound requests, host and user details, credentials, keystroke capture, execution, encoding, persistence, or reviewer and agent-override language. The patterns are case-insensitive regular expressions. Most are adapted from the DataDog GuardDog YARA rules (Apache-2.0). Excerpts that match more groups are kept first. The view is limited to one part's size, and excerpts that do not fit are counted in a note. The view is skipped for a Version with one part and for a Version at the 16-part limit. Pattern selection can miss code, so the numbered parts still hold all of the content. The view's result feeds the composite score, but it is not listed as a chunk, and the chunk and assessed-chunk counts cover only the numbered parts.
  • Call budget. A run makes at most 16 Jev requests, including the evidence view. Each halving reserves two of them.
  • Concurrency. At most 16 requests are in flight at once, and at most 1,000 start per minute. These limits apply to the whole controller, and branch bump classification shares them.

Scored parts are combined into the Version's jevAssessment fields as follows. A part whose risk level is not a known label counts as a failed part.

Field Combined as riskLevel The worst part. riskScore The highest part. The six risk probabilities The highest part for each probability. safeProbability The lowest part. riskConfidence The lowest part. model The model of the worst part.

Before the parts are combined, each scored part also gets a composite risk. The composite is a logistic regression over Jev's answers for the safe probability, the risk confidence, and the prompt injection, data exfiltration, destructive actions, hidden instructions, and remote execution probabilities. It estimates the chance that the part is malicious. That chance is scaled to the 0 to 4 score scale by multiplying by 5 and capping at 4, so a chance of 0.5 is High and a chance of 0.7 or more is Critical. Scope mismatch is not an input, so it cannot raise a part on its own. The coefficients were fit on 300 samples from public benchmarks, outside their sealed test partitions: 150 malicious and 150 benign. Most malicious samples come from MaliciousSkillBench (code Apache-2.0; metadata CC BY 4.0) and SkillTrustBench. Nearly all benign samples come from SkillTrustBench and AgentTrap, so the fit reflects those sources more than the general population of skills. They are fixed in the controller. The coefficients depend on the current question wording. Some of that wording, including the explicit lists of what is and is not a finding, was adapted from the Cisco AI Defense skill-scanner (Apache-2.0).

A scored part's level becomes the label nearest its composite score when that label is higher than Jev's own label. The composite can only raise a part's risk score and level. It never lowers Jev's own answer. The raised values flow into the chunk chips, the combined riskLevel, and the threshold and Critical checks. A strong combination of prompt injection and hidden instructions can raise a part to Critical. Exfiltration on its own does not raise a part, because the fitted coefficient for it is near zero.

The composite's accuracy is limited to the sources it was fit on, and it does not transfer reliably to other sources. On the sealed MaliciousSkillBench test partition, which the coefficients never saw, 28% of malicious parts reached High or higher, and 8% of benign parts did. The question wording was adjusted on samples that include 12 test-partition members, so that result is not fully clean. On two held-out malicious sources the composite reached High or higher for 30% (SRC004) and 3% (SRC005) of samples. Benign samples for those sources were not available, so their false-positive rate is unknown.

A second composite was fit on the full train and validation splits, with the original question wording, and tested once on the same sealed partition. It flagged 24% of malicious parts and 17% of benign parts at High or higher, with an AUC of 0.70. Benign false positives varied by source, from 2% to 90%, and the fit depended heavily on the hidden instructions probe. That composite is not in the controller, and the shipped coefficients are unchanged. Treat a risk level as a triage signal, not a verdict.

To check benign false positives outside the fit sources, 250 benign skills from awesome-copilot (MIT) were scored with the shipped coefficients. None of them were used to fit those coefficients. Of the first 150, 1.3% reached High or higher. A later set of 100, chosen so it did not overlap the first 150, gave 2 High or higher out of 95 usable skills (2.1%). The first 150 were also used to compare refit coefficients, so the second set is the cleaner estimate. Both sets cover benign skills only, so they do not measure malicious recall.

docs.title: Thresholds
docs.text:
The jevPolicy thresholds decide whether a Version is blocked. Each threshold is optional. Each threshold is checked against every part, and a breach in any part blocks the Version.

Threshold Blocks when minSafeProbability The safe probability is below the value. maxInjectionProbability The injection probability is above the value. maxExfiltrationProbability The exfiltration probability is above the value. maxDestructiveProbability The destructive probability is above the value. maxHiddenInstructionsProbability The hidden instructions probability is above the value. maxScopeMismatchProbability The scope mismatch probability is above the value. maxRemoteExecutionProbability The remote execution probability is above the value. maxRiskScore The risk score is above the value. minConfidence The riskConfidence of any part is below the value. Also sets needsReview.

The gate follows these rules:

  • Thresholds block when breached. A threshold that is not set never blocks a Version. A RiskLevel of Critical always blocks, whatever the thresholds are.
  • Critical sets needsReview. A Critical risk level also sets needsReview. It is set when every part is scored. An assessment that ends early, for a Service failure or a token limit, does not set it, even when a part is Critical.
  • Fail closed whenever Jev is configured. A source that sets jevSecretRef blocks its Version on a Service failure, with or without thresholds. A Service failure is a part that Jev fails to score, a token Secret that cannot be read, or a read error on the extracted content. The error is recorded in status.jevAssessment.error. See Retries.
  • Content outcomes block without an error. These block the Version with or without thresholds. They record no error, and they are not retried:
    • The content needs more than 16 parts. No Jev call is made.
    • The content cannot be read for splitting.
    • A binary file, which has a NUL byte or invalid UTF-8. No Jev call is made.
    • A file that the Trivy secret scanner flags. The file is withheld, and no Jev call is made.
    • A part that Jev rejects for its token limit, when the part cannot be split further or no call budget is left, and no other part failed.
  • Jev disabled blocks sources that set jevSecretRef. When Jev is disabled on the controller (scanning.jev.enabled: false), a source that sets jevSecretRef is blocked. No Jev call is made, and this is not counted as a retry.

Assessments are cached in status.jevAssessment. A completed assessment is reused. Set forceSync: true on the Version that the Skill or Agent points to, not on the Skill or Agent itself, to run a new assessment. A completed assessment from before this release is reused unchanged.

docs.title: Score colors
docs.text:
The Jev panel colors each probability bar by risk, using the same bands as the CLI output (cli/output.go). For the Safe row, risk is 1 − safe probability. Every other row uses its probability as the risk.

Band Risk Red 0.50 or higher Yellow 0.25 to below 0.50 Green Below 0.25

For the Safe row, a value above 0.75 is green, and a value of 0.50 or lower is red. A bar is always red when its threshold is breached, regardless of its band. The risk level uses the same colors: Minimal and Low are green, Moderate is yellow, and High and Critical are red.

The Jev panel on a Skill or Agent Version shows the overall risk, the risk score, the confidence, and a probability bar for each question. The accessibility Agent Version below has a Low risk level with a 0.69 risk score and 88.0% confidence. Every probability bar is green:

The gh-actions-debug Skill Version below has a Low risk level with a 1.45 risk score and 32.0% confidence. Its safe and destructive actions bars are yellow:

docs.title: Needs review
docs.text: Open Needs review in the sidebar to list Skills and Agents whose jevAssessment.needsReview is true. The list reads only each resource's latest-assessed Version, so an older Version that needs review is not listed.

docs.title: Data handling
docs.text:
When Jev is enabled and a source sets jevSecretRef, the controller sends one request per part to the Jev endpoint. A Version has at most 16 parts. See How content is split. The content is sent as follows:

  • Sent: the entry file (SKILL.md or the agent .md file), the list of file names bundled with the Version, and all text content of the bundled files. Nothing is cut for size. Scripts and bundled text files are sent, each under a --- <path> --- delimiter.
  • Not sent: binary files (a NUL byte or invalid UTF-8), which are replaced by [skipped: binary file]. A binary file blocks the Version, and no Jev call is made.
  • Withheld: bundled text files that the Trivy secret scanner flags are replaced by [withheld: flagged for a secret] and are not sent to Jev. The entry file is replaced by [withheld: entry file flagged for a secret] and is not sent to Jev. A withheld file blocks the Version, and no Jev call is made, whatever the thresholds.
  • Never sent: the Jev token. The token is only used as the request credential and is never logged or written to a resource.

Before you use Jev on private repositories, get the TypeSafe retention and training terms in writing. Confirm how long TypeSafe keeps submitted content and whether it is used for model training. Do not enable Jev for private source until those terms are confirmed.

docs.title: Assessed content
docs.text:
The assessed content view in the Jev panel has two views, switched with the Files and Chunks toggle. Files shows a directory tree. Each file shows its risk level and the parts that contain it, such as 3 and 3a. When a part that holds a file did not score, the file shows that part's status. Chunks lists the parts sorted by index. Each row shows the part's status, risk level, score, and confidence. Skipped files are listed below the parts. When a part's file list was cut, the view shows how many files are not listed.

The Jev panel also shows an estimated input cost when a Version has status.jevAssessment.inputTokens. The value is the sum of the input tokens that Jev reports for every call that returned usage, across all parts. This includes parts that Jev later marked as failed, because Jev still bills them. A call that fails without usage is not counted. The UI estimates the cost at $0.042 per million input tokens. Output tokens are not included. The Stats page shows the same estimate as a lifetime total across visible Versions, so deleting a Version also removes its cost from the total. Update the rate in services/ui/src/lib/jevCost.ts if Jev pricing changes.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Jev digest, exemptions, and retries: read a digest, clear a Jev block, and understand retries.
  • Scanning configuration: the Jev policy and scan settings.

docs.title: Publishing Agents and Skills
docs.text: This guide covers how Skills and Agents are published from Git: as Skill and Agent resources in a GitOps workflow or through a Depot. It also covers the agent service, the source configuration, branch sourcing, version bumps, and definition storage. Each Version passes the deterministic checks and, when enabled, the Jev assessment before it is served. To install these resources, see Consuming Agents and Skills.

docs.title: Agent service
docs.text:
The agent service is disabled by default. Enable it with agent.enabled: true in the chart values. The agent deployment runs with these security settings:

  • seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault
  • runAsNonRoot: true
  • All Linux capabilities dropped (drop: [ALL])
  • A CPU limit of 500m by default

docs.title: Publishing Skill and Agent resources with GitOps
docs.text:
A Skill or Agent resource does not require a Depot. Declare it in Git and let your GitOps tool, such as Argo CD, apply it. The agentSourceConfig fields are the same ones a Depot entry uses.

A standalone resource does not discover versions. Each entry in versions must name a version explicitly, and that version must match an existing Git tag. The version controller looks for the tag v1.0.0 or 1.0.0, with tagPrefix in front when it is set. Only a Depot discovers Git tags for a version range and follows branch commits, so a standalone resource cannot use ref.

apiVersion: opendepot.defdev.io/v1alpha1
kind: Skill
metadata:
  name: code-review
  namespace: opendepot-system
spec:
  agentSourceConfig:
    repoOwner: my-org
    repoUrl: https://github.com/my-org/skills
    path: skills/code-review
  versions:
    - version: 1.0.0

For an Agent, set path to the agent definition file, such as agents/code-reviewer.agent.md.

docs.title: Publishing with a Depot
docs.text:
A Depot can also publish skills and agents on your behalf through the skillConfigs and agentConfigs fields. It creates the Skill and Agent resources for you.

A Depot publishes skills and agents through the skillConfigs and agentConfigs fields. Each entry references a Git repository that holds a SKILL.md file (for skills) or an agent file (for agents). An agent file is accepted as {name}.agent.md, the Copilot layout, {name}.md, the Claude layout, or {name}.toml, the Codex layout. A source directory that contains both files for the same agent is rejected as ambiguous. The agent's name in its frontmatter is display metadata. It may be any non-empty string up to 64 characters. The file name is the registry identifier, so the name in the Agent configuration must match the file name without the .agent.md, .md, or .toml suffix. For example, code-reviewer matches code-reviewer.agent.md.

apiVersion: opendepot.defdev.io/v1alpha1
kind: Depot
metadata:
  name: team-agents
  namespace: opendepot-system
spec:
  skillConfigs:
    - name: release-notes
      repoOwner: my-org
      repoUrl: https://github.com/my-org/release-notes-skill
      path: skills/release-notes
      versionConstraints: ">= 1.0.0"
      versionHistoryLimit: 5
      storageConfig:
        s3:
          bucket: opendepot-artifacts
          region: us-east-1
  agentConfigs:
    - name: code-reviewer
      repoOwner: my-org
      repoUrl: https://github.com/my-org/code-reviewer-agent
      path: agents/code-reviewer
      versionConstraints: "~> 2.1"
      storageConfig:
        s3:
          bucket: opendepot-artifacts
          region: us-east-1

Each entry accepts the same source fields as other OpenDepot sources:

Field Purpose name The skill or agent name. Defaults to the Skill or Agent resource name when omitted. repoOwner, repoUrl The GitHub repository that holds the source. The owner and repository names must match ^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,100}$. path For a skill, the directory that holds SKILL.md. For an agent, either the directory that holds the agent definition or the definition file itself, such as agents/code-reviewer.agent.md. A file path bundles only that file. platform The agent platform whose frontmatter keys are enforced. One of agentskills, claude, copilot, codex, opencode, or pi. Optional. See Frontmatter validation. tagPrefix A prefix that Git tags must have to be considered versions. The prefix may contain /, for example skills/. versionConstraints A version constraint applied to the discovered Git tags. Tag mode only. Mutually exclusive with ref. ref A Git branch to follow instead of tags. Enables branch sourcing. Mutually exclusive with versionConstraints and tagPrefix. branchPolicy Branch-mode thresholds and the minimum interval between Versions. Requires ref. See Version bump classification. versionHistoryLimit How many synced versions are kept. immutable Prevents a published version from being changed. storageConfig Where the packaged archive, checksums, and signature are stored. githubClientConfig A GitHub App credential reference for private repositories. jevSecretRef and jevPolicy Optional TypeSafe Jev assessment. See Jev assessment.

GitHub inputs are validated before any API request is made. repoOwner and the repository name must match ^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,100}$. A Git ref, including a tag, is checked one /-separated segment at a time. Each segment must match ^[A-Za-z0-9._+-]{1,200}$. Empty segments and the . and .. segments are rejected, and so are characters such as ?, #, %, @, and \. If a tag fails these rules, the archive fetch fails and the Version is not synced.

The version controller packages each matching Git tag into an archive, signs the SHA256SUMS file with the configured GPG key, and runs the deterministic checks before a Version is marked synced. The server exposes the results through the agents.v1 protocol. For the endpoints, see agents.v1 protocol. For install steps, see the CLI reference.

The signing key is configured through the version.gpg.secretName Secret, which must hold OPENDEPOT_PROVIDER_GPG_PRIVATE_KEY_BASE64 with an unprotected (no passphrase) armored private key. The server reads the same variable from the server.gpg Secret and derives the fingerprint from it. The version.gpg and server.gpg Secrets must hold the same key. If the derived fingerprint does not match the one recorded on the Version, the server returns HTTP 500 and refuses to serve signing material.

docs.title: Branch sourcing
docs.text:
Set ref on a skill or agent source to follow a Git branch instead of publishing from tags. Only a Depot discovers branch commits, so set ref in skillConfigs or agentConfigs. A standalone Skill or Agent resource cannot follow a branch. Branch sourcing is off by default. It is enabled only when the chart is installed with branchSourcing.enabled: true, which sets --branch-sourcing-enabled on the depot and version controllers.

skillConfigs:
  - name: release-notes
    repoOwner: my-org
    repoUrl: https://github.com/my-org/release-notes-skill
    path: skills/release-notes
    ref: main
    branchPolicy:
      minVersionInterval: 10m
    storageConfig:
      s3:
        bucket: opendepot-artifacts
        region: us-east-1

ref and versionConstraints are mutually exclusive, and so are ref and tagPrefix. branchPolicy applies only to branch sources and requires ref.

Tags are usually more immutable than branches, so tag mode is the recommended default for stable content. A branch head moves with every push. Each Version is still pinned to its exact sourceCommit, so consumers always receive the content of a specific commit.

  • Pushing publishes. A push to the branch publishes a new Version once all checks pass. Protect the branch with required reviews and status checks, because anyone who can push to it can publish.
  • Each new commit is a new Version. A Version is named <prefix>-<configName>-<40-char SHA> and is labeled opendepot.defdev.io/commit. It stays Pending until the version controller assigns it a semver after signing. A source has at most one Pending entry at a time.
  • Polling is opt-in. A branch source picks up new commits on a schedule only when pollingIntervalMinutes is set on the Depot. When it is unset, a branch source picks up new commits only when the Depot reconciles for another reason, such as a spec change, an annotation change, or a resync. See Polling interval.
  • immutable works on branch sources. Each Version is pinned to its sourceCommit, and a re-download must match its recorded status.checksum. A moving branch creates new Versions and does not change existing ones. The checksum is stable only while the archive format is stable, so a packaging change can alter it for the same SHA, the same as with tags.
  • Recreating a source resets numbering. Deleting and recreating a source starts semver numbering again. Consumer lock hashes recorded against the old numbering then fail closed.

Branch sources are intended as a one-time migration. After the migration, manage the source definitions through GitOps.

docs.title: Version bump classification
docs.text:
In branch mode, the version controller chooses the semver bump for each new commit. The deterministic checks and Trivy scans run first. Jev runs only after they pass. The 43 KiB state cap also applies to bump classification, so a long diff can be truncated before Jev sees it.

  • A flagged entry file means MAJOR. When the entry file is flagged, the bump is MAJOR with source Withheld, and Jev is not called. A flagged file that is not the entry file is shown as <path> (content withheld).
  • Thresholds set the bump. The Jev probabilities are compared against branchPolicy:
    • MAJOR when the major-change probability is at least majorThreshold.
    • MINOR when the major-change probability plus the minor-change probability is at least minorThreshold.
    • PATCH otherwise.
  • Low confidence means review. A Version whose confidence is below minConfidence is marked needsReview. This is informational only and never blocks a Version.

When Jev is not used for a bump, the result is PATCH with source Default:

  • No jevSecretRef is set on the source.
  • scanning.jev.enabled is false, which sets --jev-enabled=false.

When Jev is enabled and a call used to classify a bump for a later commit fails, the Version is Held and is not published as PATCH. The version controller retries with a capped backoff of 1, 2, 4, 8, and then 15 minutes. Bump calls share the limit of 16 in-flight Jev requests and the rate limit of 1,000 per minute with Jev assessments across the controller.

Set the opendepot.defdev.io/bump-override annotation on a Version to major, minor, or patch to override the bump size. The override is recorded with source Manual. It is honored only while the Version is Pending or Held. It sets the bump size only and does not decide whether the Version is published. It does not release a hold caused by a missing jevSecretRef; set jevSecretRef on the source to publish.

docs.title: Definition storage
docs.text:
Each Skill and Agent Version stores its definition file in a ConfigMap of its own. The ConfigMap is referenced by status.definitionConfigMapRef and is owned by the Version, so it is deleted with the Version. The UI renders the file as SKILL.md for skills and AGENT.md for agents. Module READMEs use a separate reference, readmeConfigMapRef, which applies only to modules. Skill and Agent Versions never fill README content.

The definition is stored base64 encoded. The encoded data must be at most 1,000,000 bytes, which keeps it under the 1 MiB ConfigMap limit. A larger definition is not synced. The Version gets synced: false and a syncStatus message that gives the file name, its size, the encoded size, and the limit, for example:

definition exceeds the ConfigMap size limit: definition file SKILL.md is 800000 bytes, which encodes to 1066668 bytes against a 1000000 byte limit

The Version stays unsynced until the definition changes.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text: • Name collisions. Version names use a prefix-name-version pattern without escaping. A Skill and an Agent that produce the same Version name can collide. A collision returns 404 and never serves the wrong object.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Skill and Agent checks: the checks that run before a Version is synced.
  • Jev assessment: optional AI assessment of each Version.
  • Assembly Line: automate Depot publishing.
  • GroupBinding Access Control: control which subjects can read skills and agents.

docs.title: Consuming Agents and Skills
docs.text: OpenDepot publishes Agent Skills and Agents from Git repositories. Install them into a project with the opendepot CLI, which verifies signatures and hashes before anything is written to disk. To publish them, see Publishing Agents and Skills.

docs.title: Install with the CLI
docs.text:
Install the opendepot binary first. The CLI reference shows how to download it from the registry and verify the checksum.

opendepot login registry.example.com
opendepot list skills
opendepot describe skill my-org/release-notes
opendepot plan
opendepot apply
opendepot verify
  • opendepot list skills and opendepot list agents show what a registry offers. Listing is read-only.
  • opendepot describe skill <namespace/name> or opendepot describe agent <namespace/name> shows the versions, rejection reasons, and latest Jev assessment for one resource.
  • opendepot plan shows what apply would change without writing anything.
  • opendepot apply installs every entry in opendepot.hcl.
  • opendepot verify checks the installed targets against opendepot.lock.hcl without network access.

For every command and flag, see the CLI reference.

docs.title: Browse view
docs.text:
The UI browse view shows the sync status of each Version. It also shows blocked and unsynced Versions, and the scan and Jev findings for them. Anyone who can see the parent Agent or Skill can see this data. Browse is filtered per Agent through the caller's GroupBinding. This is intentional, so operators can see why a Version was blocked.

For a Skill or Agent that follows a branch, the detail header shows the source repository, the tracked branch, and the source path. It also shows the latest commit as a 7-character SHA. The Versions table lists every Version, including branch Versions in the Pending and Held phases. Each row shows its commit with a copy button and a branch phase chip. The commit column appears when at least one row has a commit. A Version without a semver shows —. See Agent Details and Skill Details for the full page layout.

The presign setting on an Agent or Skill source is copied to each Version it owns. Changing presign on the source updates every existing Version on the next reconcile, including yanked and rejected Versions. Removing presign from the source clears it on the Versions. Manual edits to a Version's presign are overwritten to match the source. Other Version fields are not changed by this sync.

docs.title: Yanked and blocked Versions
docs.text:
Yank a Version by setting spec.yanked: true on the Version resource. Yanked Versions stay listed and downloadable, and the listing includes yanked: true. The CLI skips yanked Versions when it resolves a version constraint unless you pass --allow-yanked.

A Version that Jev blocks is listed with blocked: true and its blockReasons, so clients can explain why it is unavailable. It is never served, and a direct download request for it returns 404. The CLI skips blocked Versions when it resolves a version constraint. Causes include a threshold breach, a Critical risk level, a Service failure, a content outcome, and Jev disabled on the controller while jevSecretRef is set.

docs.title: Unavailable candidates
docs.text:
The versions response can include unavailableCandidates. It lists newer Versions that match the constraint but cannot be installed, so clients can explain why the newest matching Version is missing. The field is optional and is omitted when there are none. Servers that predate it never send it, so clients must treat a missing field as not reported, not as no candidates.

Each entry has these fields:

Field Purpose version The version of a versioned candidate. Omitted for an unversioned commit. commit The source commit of an unversioned candidate. Omitted for a versioned candidate. status One of blocked, rejected, pending, or assessmentFailed. reasons Sanitized text. Jev block reasons are passed through for Jev-blocked candidates. All other reasons are fixed messages. Raw sync status is never returned. Status Meaning blocked A Jev policy blocks the Version. rejected A scan policy rejected the Version, or the branch lifecycle rejected the commit. An unversioned commit that Jev blocks is also reported as rejected. assessmentFailed Syncing or assessing the Version failed. pending An unversioned commit is waiting for an older commit to be assessed, for a version assignment, or for its first assessment.

Installable Versions stay in versions. A blocked Version is listed in versions with blocked: true when its parent ref is synced. Otherwise it appears only in unavailableCandidates. Entries are sorted by version, then commit, then status.

The CLI uses this field to decide whether an older-version fallback needs --allow-older-versions. See Allow older versions.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Verify with Agent Hooks: run opendepot verify before each agent tool call in Claude Code, Codex, and Copilot.
  • OpenDepot CLI skill: a skill that helps agents use the CLI. A raw copy is at SKILL.md.
  • CLI reference: commands, flags, and install targets.
  • agents.v1 protocol: the endpoints the CLI calls.
  • Publishing Agents and Skills: configure a Depot to publish skills and agents.
  • GroupBinding Access Control: control which subjects can read skills and agents.

docs.title: Assembly Line
docs.text:
Assembly Line composes onboarded OpenDepot modules and providers into a validated OpenTofu root module, directly in the browser. An administrator must enable it first; see Assembly Line Configuration.

Assembly Line is OpenTofu-only and browser-local/export-only: canvases persist in the browser's localStorage (nothing is saved server-side), and the only server-side artifact is the validated ZIP produced at export time.

docs.title: The Assembly Line Workflow
docs.text:
Assembly Line turns a visual canvas into a portable OpenTofu root module:

  1. Add a module, provider, or variable from the resource palette.
  2. Configure inputs and provider arguments from the node panels.
  3. Wire variables and module outputs to downstream inputs.
  4. Choose count or for_each when a module should produce multiple instances.
  5. Export the validated main.tf and variables.tf files.

docs.title: Build a Root Module
docs.text:
Module and provider nodes select an onboarded release. Export emits module releases as pessimistic constraints and provider releases as exact versions. Inputs and provider arguments render only when set on the canvas, so child-module and provider defaults stay in the child configuration.

Variable nodes become declarations in variables.tf. A default is emitted only when the canvas defines one. Collection, tuple, object, and optional object types are preserved.

A root variable or module output can connect to a module input or provider argument. References to repeated modules require an explicit all, index, or key selector.

Only versions with an extracted Assembly artifact appear on the canvas. See Assembly Line Configuration for administrator requirements.

docs.title: Define Complex Variables
docs.text:
Open Type on a variable node to pick a primitive, collection, tuple, or object type. Add nested attributes and optional or default values in the type editor. The HCL preview updates as you build the type.

This map's values contain a nested spec object with description and timeout attributes. Each key identifies one for_each instance, and each value holds that instance's configuration.

docs.title: Validate Variable Values
docs.text:
Add validations to reject invalid input. Each validation has two parts:

  • A condition written as an HCL expression, such as alltrue([for _, function in var.lambda_functions : length(function.spec.description) <= 100]).
  • An error message that explains how to correct the value.

The HCL preview renders the validation block in the exported variables.tf.

docs.title: Configure Module Inputs
docs.text:
Select Inputs on a module node to open its typed input form. Each row shows whether the input is required, its type, and its value controls. The generated module HCL stays visible beside the form. Use search and pagination for modules with many inputs.

Enter literal values or HCL expressions. When a field contains a supported OpenTofu function, the editor shows its description and a link to the OpenTofu documentation.

Values can come from several places:

  • A literal value entered in the form.
  • A root variable such as var.account_id.
  • A module output such as module.ecr.repo_url.
  • A repeated value such as each.key or each.value.spec.description.

To reference a root variable or module output, choose Use input and select a source. Repeated or collection sources add instance selectors and key or index controls.

Repeated modules can also use each.key and each.value in expression fields. For example, this description input reads a nested value from the current for_each object:

For a variable map or collection reference, choose One instance and enter the index or key expression to select one entry. When the selected entry is an object, optionally choose a descendant property. For example, selecting var.lambda_functions, One instance, each.key, and spec produces:

var.lambda_functions[each.key].spec

Leave the descendant selection at Whole value to reference the complete entry. All instances clears the descendant selection and passes the full collection. Type checks use the selected entry or projected property type.

docs.title: Repeat Modules with count or for_each
docs.text:
New module nodes start in single mode. To create multiple instances, open Repeat this module with count or for_each and choose the mode that matches your input.

With count, choose Fixed number to create the specified number of instances. Choose Conditional (create or not) to create either zero or one instance from a boolean condition. Fixed-count instances use numeric indexes such as module.lambda[0]; conditional instances use the same indexed form when they exist.

docs.title: Use for_each for Keyed Instances
docs.text:
Use for_each when each instance needs a stable key and its own value. Connect a map or set variable to the module's repetition input. In the example canvas, var.lambda_functions drives the Lambda, IAM, and ECR modules.

Each repeated module exposes the standard OpenTofu instance context:

  • each.key is the map key or set member identifying the current instance.
  • each.value is the object or value associated with that key.

Use each.value to populate instance-specific inputs, for example:

description = each.value.spec.description

Use each.key when the key itself is the useful value, such as a function name:

function_name = each.key

The UI only offers each.* expressions where the surrounding node is repeated, so the generated configuration remains valid OpenTofu.

docs.title: Connect Repeated Outputs
docs.text:
When a repeated module output is a map, Assembly Line asks how to select it. Choose All instances to pass the complete map, or One instance and provide a key expression such as each.key to select the matching value.

For example, a repeated IAM module can provide one role ARN per function:

iam_role_arn = module.lambda_roles[each.key].role_arns[each.key]

The same selector appears when connecting an output from a repeated ECR module:

image_uri = module.ecr[each.key].repo_url

Each Lambda instance stays paired with its own IAM role and container image.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
Provider nodes must reference onboarded OpenDepot Provider resources with an extracted configuration schema. Configure required and optional attributes and nested blocks from that schema.

A module's provider selector lists only provider nodes whose upstream identity matches the module contract. For example, a module requirement for hashicorp/aws can bind to an onboarded OpenDepot Provider whose providerNamespace/name is hashicorp/aws.

Multiple configurations of one provider share one required_providers entry. Give additional configurations an alias, then bind each module-local provider name to the appropriate root configuration.

Select Configuration on a provider node to set arguments from the extracted schema. The form marks optional attributes and shows complex types such as set(string). Add or remove nested blocks such as assume_role inline. Provider values accept the same typed references as module inputs.

Provider configuration belongs on the root provider node. Modules then select the matching provider configuration through their Providers panel, keeping provider setup separate from module input wiring.

docs.title: OpenTofu-only eligibility
docs.text:
OpenDepot's provider registry generally mirrors both registry.opentofu.org and registry.terraform.io origins (see Consuming Providers). Assembly Line is narrower: it only supports providers whose spec.providerConfig.upstreamRegistry resolves to registry.opentofu.org.

  • The /assembly provider palette in the UI filters out any Provider whose upstream registry is not registry.opentofu.org, so Terraform-origin providers never appear as candidates.
  • Export resolution enforces the same rule authoritatively on the server: a canvas that references a non-OpenTofu Provider fails with a provider_registry_unsupported diagnostic, regardless of what the browser submitted.

When Assembly Line is enabled, the Version controller extracts a configuration schema for each provider version, regardless of upstream registry. Providers from both origins remain usable outside Assembly Line.

docs.title: Generated provider source
docs.text:
Generated provider source addresses use the provider's canonical short identity, never the OpenDepot host:

<providerNamespace>/<providerName>

For example, an onboarded Provider with providerNamespace: hashicorp and providerName: aws renders source = "hashicorp/aws" in required_providers. OpenDepot is only the installation location configured in the generated OpenTofu CLI config, never the provider's identity in HCL.

Generated module source addresses continue to use the OpenDepot module registry host:

<ui.baseUrl host>/<kubernetes namespace>/<Module resource name>/<provider system>

Module versions are emitted as pessimistic constraints without a leading v. For example, selecting module version 1.1.1 produces:

version = "~> 1.1.1"

Provider versions remain exact and are emitted without a leading v.

docs.title: Export
docs.text: Export sends the canvas to the server, which validates it, resolves the selected versions, runs OpenTofu initialization, and returns a ZIP of the root module. Validation failures appear in the export dialog, and no ZIP is returned.

docs.title: Downloaded files
docs.text:
A successful download is named assembly-line.zip and contains exactly:

main.tf
variables.tf

The archive excludes .terraform, lock files, state, CLI configuration, command output, and all other temporary files.

docs.title: Export Failures
docs.text:
The browser blocks export while nodes are loading or have name, input, provider, reference, or multiplicity errors. Server diagnostics include a stable error code, the node, and the field path where available, such as provider_registry_unsupported for a non-OpenTofu provider.

The server returns no ZIP when resource authorization, exact-version resolution, provider eligibility, rendering, or OpenTofu initialization fails.

docs.title: Registry Reads with Dex Client Credentials
docs.text:
If your organization uses OIDC (Dex) for humans, pipelines can authenticate with the Dex client credentials grant. Pipelines read the registry through the server, and Kubernetes RBAC governs changes to resources.

The examples assume server-proxied Dex (server.oidc.dexProxy.enabled: true), so the token endpoint shares the registry host. If Dex is exposed separately, substitute its host (for example https://dex.defdev.io/dex/token).

Enable client credentials in your Helm values and register a dedicated Dex static client:

dex:
  config:
    oauth2:
      grantTypes:
        - authorization_code
        - client_credentials
    staticClients:
      - id: opendepot
        name: OpenDepot
        secretEnv: OPENDEPOT_DEX_CLIENT_SECRET
        redirectURIs:
          - https://opendepot.defdev.io/auth/callback
      - id: ci-pipeline
        name: CI Pipeline
        secretEnv: OPENDEPOT_CC_CLIENT_SECRET
        grantTypes:
          - client_credentials
server:
  oidc:
    enabled: true
    allowClientCredentials: true
    clientCredentialsAudiences:
      - ci-pipeline

clientCredentialsAudiences lists each Dex client ID that uses the client_credentials grant. OpenDepot rejects tokens whose aud is not on this list.

Create a GroupBinding to authorize the pipeline client:

apiVersion: opendepot.defdev.io/v1alpha1
kind: GroupBinding
metadata:
  name: ci-pipeline-binding
  namespace: opendepot-system
spec:
  expression: '"client:ci-pipeline" in groups'
  moduleResources:
    - "*"
  providerResources:
    - "*"

docs.title: GitHub Actions Example
docs.text:
jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Get Dex CC token for OpenDepot registry
        id: opendepot-token
        env:
          CC_CLIENT_SECRET: ${{ secrets.OPENDEPOT_CC_CLIENT_SECRET }}
        run: |
          TOKEN=$(curl -sf -X POST https://opendepot.defdev.io/dex/token \
            -d grant_type=client_credentials \
            -d client_id=ci-pipeline \
            -d "client_secret=${CC_CLIENT_SECRET}" \
            -d scope=openid \
            | jq -r '.access_token')
          echo "token=$TOKEN" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Write .tofurc
        run: |
          cat > ~/.tofurc <<EOF
          credentials "opendepot.defdev.io" {
            token = "${{ steps.opendepot-token.outputs.token }}"
          }

          provider_installation {
            network_mirror {
              url     = "https://opendepot.defdev.io/opendepot/providers/mirror/v1/opendepot-system/"
              include = ["registry.opentofu.org/*/*"]
            }

            direct {
              exclude = ["registry.opentofu.org/*/*"]
            }
          }
          EOF

      - name: Setup OpenTofu
        uses: opentofu/setup-opentofu@v1

      - run: tofu init

This configures OpenTofu to install providers through the Network Mirror Protocol while keeping canonical registry.opentofu.org identity in your configuration and lockfile. Dex sets the token lifetime, and access is limited to what a GroupBinding grants client:<sub>. The runner needs only network access to the Dex token endpoint, not a kubeconfig.

To use Terraform instead, rename the file to .terraformrc and replace setup-opentofu with hashicorp/setup-terraform. If your Provider resources use upstreamRegistry: registry.terraform.io, update the include and exclude patterns to registry.terraform.io/*/*.

For full configuration details see Client Credentials (Machine-to-Machine). For a side-by-side comparison of all supported authentication methods and their access-control mechanisms, see the Authentication Comparison table.

docs.title: Registry Reads: SA Fallback with OIDC
docs.text:
Last resort — exhaust other options first

SA fallback bypasses GroupBinding entirely. When a ServiceAccount token is used, the SA's Kubernetes RBAC governs access instead of the centralized GroupBinding model your OIDC setup provides. This means:

  • Human users and pipeline tokens follow different access control paths, which increases audit surface.
  • A leaked pipeline token grants direct cluster API access, not just registry access.
  • SA-token access is invisible to GroupBinding audit logs.

Before enabling SA fallback, consider whether one of these fits your use case instead:

  • Publishing modules only? → Use the GitOps approach. No pipeline credentials needed at all — Argo CD handles cluster auth, developers push to Git.
  • Reading the registry from pipelines without cluster access? → Use Dex Client Credentials. Pipelines get a Dex-issued token scoped to GroupBinding, with no Kubernetes API exposure.

SA fallback is appropriate when your pipeline must interact with the Kubernetes API directly for reasons beyond registry access and you have already ruled out the above options.

When your organization uses OIDC for human users, CI/CD pipelines still need to run tofu init and download providers from the registry. Without a fallback, pipelines need a separate credential mechanism. The ServiceAccount fallback removes this constraint.

docs.title: Enable SA Fallback in Your Helm Values
docs.text:
server:
  oidc:
    enabled: true
    allowServiceAccountFallback: true

This lets K8s SA tokens authenticate alongside OIDC JWTs. SA tokens bypass GroupBinding and rely on Kubernetes RBAC directly.

docs.title: Create an SA and Bind Registry-Reader RBAC
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: ci-registry-reader
  namespace: my-ci-namespace
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: opendepot-registry-reader
  namespace: opendepot-system
rules:
- apiGroups: ["opendepot.defdev.io"]
  resources: ["modules", "versions", "providers"]
  verbs: ["get", "list"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: opendepot-registry-reader-binding
  namespace: opendepot-system
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: opendepot-registry-reader
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: ci-registry-reader
  namespace: my-ci-namespace

docs.title: GitHub Actions Example
docs.text:
jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      id-token: write  # required for OIDC to your cloud provider
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Configure AWS credentials
        uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::<ACCOUNT>:role/my-role
          aws-region: us-west-2

      - name: Configure kubeconfig for EKS
        run: aws eks update-kubeconfig --name my-cluster --region us-west-2

      - name: Get SA token for OpenDepot registry
        id: opendepot-token
        run: |
          TOKEN=$(kubectl create token ci-registry-reader \
            -n my-ci-namespace \
            --duration=15m)
          echo "token=$TOKEN" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Write .tofurc
        run: |
          cat > ~/.tofurc <<EOF
          credentials "opendepot.defdev.io" {
            token = "${{ steps.opendepot-token.outputs.token }}"
          }

          provider_installation {
            network_mirror {
              url     = "https://opendepot.defdev.io/opendepot/providers/mirror/v1/opendepot-system/"
              include = ["registry.opentofu.org/*/*"]
            }

            direct {
              exclude = ["registry.opentofu.org/*/*"]
            }
          }
          EOF

      - name: Setup OpenTofu
        uses: opentofu/setup-opentofu@v1

      - run: tofu init

This configures OpenTofu to install providers through the Network Mirror Protocol while keeping canonical registry.opentofu.org identity. For Terraform, see the note in the Dex section above. The --duration=15m token expires quickly, and RBAC limits what it can read, whatever the runner's cloud IAM role allows. If the runner's identity already has suitable Kubernetes RBAC, you can use its token instead. See Managed Cluster Tokens.

docs.title: Push-Based Workflows
docs.text:
For private modules you control, bypass the Depot entirely and create Module resources directly from your CI/CD pipeline:

apiVersion: opendepot.defdev.io/v1alpha1
kind: Module
metadata:
  name: terraform-aws-eks
  namespace: opendepot-system
spec:
  moduleConfig:
    name: terraform-aws-eks
    provider: aws
    repoOwner: terraform-aws-modules
    repoUrl: https://github.com/terraform-aws-modules/terraform-aws-eks
    fileFormat: zip
    immutable: true
    storageConfig:
      s3:
        bucket: opendepot-modules
        region: us-west-2
    githubClientConfig:
      useAuthenticatedClient: true
  versions:
    - version: "21.10.1"
    - version: "21.11.0"
    - version: "21.12.0"

GitHub Actions Example:

name: Publish Module Version

on:
  release:
    types: [published]

jobs:
  publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Configure AWS credentials
        uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>:role/opendepot-github-actions-role
          aws-region: us-west-2

      - name: Setup kubeconfig
        run: aws eks update-kubeconfig --name my-cluster --region us-west-2

      - name: Publish module version
        run: |
          kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
          apiVersion: opendepot.defdev.io/v1alpha1
          kind: Module
          metadata:
            name: my-module
            namespace: opendepot-system
          spec:
            moduleConfig:
              name: my-module
              provider: aws
              repoOwner: my-org
              repoUrl: https://github.com/my-org/terraform-aws-my-module
              fileFormat: zip
              storageConfig:
                s3:
                  bucket: opendepot-modules
                  region: us-west-2
            versions:
              - version: ${{ github.event.release.tag_name }}
          EOF

The Module controller creates the Version resource, and the Version controller fetches the archive from GitHub and uploads it to storage — no manual archive upload needed.

To publish subsequent versions of an existing module from a pipeline, see Adding versions to an existing module.

docs.title: Related Admin Operations
docs.text: For day-2 operations, see Registry Operations. For configuration reference, see Vulnerability Scanning and Pre-signed URL Redirects.

docs.title: Pull-Based Workflow: Using the Depot
docs.text:
The Depot is a pull-based controller. It discovers, downloads, and tracks modules, providers, Skills, and Agents from external sources, so your registry stays current without manual imports.

Use it for:

  • Upstream provider mirroring: sync providers from the OpenTofu or Terraform Registry into your storage backend, and pick up new releases on a schedule
  • Public module tracking: follow open-source modules by GitHub repository, and pin or float versions with constraints
  • Private module import: pull from private GitHub repositories with GitHub App authentication. This is also the starting point for migrating to OpenDepot.

docs.title: Syncing upstream providers
docs.text:
Mirrored providers keep their canonical identity (for example registry.opentofu.org/hashicorp/aws). Configurations reference the canonical source, and OpenDepot serves it through the Network Mirror Protocol. Set the source with spec.providerConfigs[].upstreamRegistry, which defaults to registry.opentofu.org. See Consuming Providers for .tofurc examples.

apiVersion: opendepot.defdev.io/v1alpha1
kind: Depot
metadata:
  name: upstream-providers
  namespace: opendepot-system
spec:
  global:
    storageConfig:
      s3:
        bucket: opendepot-providers
        region: us-east-1
  providerConfigs:
    - name: aws
      operatingSystems:
        - linux
      architectures:
        - amd64
        - arm64
      versionConstraints: ">= 5.80.0"
    - name: azurerm
      operatingSystems:
        - linux
      architectures:
        - amd64
        - arm64
      versionConstraints: ">= 4.0.0"
    - name: google
      operatingSystems:
        - linux
      architectures:
        - amd64
        - arm64
      versionConstraints: ">= 6.0.0"
  pollingIntervalMinutes: 1440

The Depot queries the upstream registry for each provider, filters releases by version constraint, and creates Provider and Version resources for each matching OS and architecture. When scanning is enabled, the Version controller runs a binary scan (trivy rootfs) on each binary. It also runs a source scan (trivy fs on the provider's go.mod) when the repository is resolvable. If the go.mod cannot be downloaded, no source scan is stored and the Version retries.

To mirror from registry.terraform.io instead, set the upstreamRegistry field explicitly:

providerConfigs:
  - name: aws
    upstreamRegistry: registry.terraform.io
    operatingSystems:
      - linux
    architectures:
      - amd64
      - arm64
    versionConstraints: ">= 5.80.0"

With pollingIntervalMinutes: 1440, the Depot checks for new releases daily and creates matching resources automatically.

Tip

">= 5.80.0" tracks every release above a known baseline. "~> 5.80" stays on the 5.x line and excludes major upgrades.

Note

Provider names default to the hashicorp namespace. To mirror a provider from a different registry namespace (e.g., DataDog/datadog or integrations/github), set the namespace field explicitly: 

providerConfigs:
  - name: datadog
    namespace: DataDog
    versionConstraints: ">= 3.50.0"

docs.title: Tracking public modules
docs.text:
Point the Depot at an upstream GitHub repository and set a version constraint to control which module versions reach your registry.

apiVersion: opendepot.defdev.io/v1alpha1
kind: Depot
metadata:
  name: public-modules
  namespace: opendepot-system
spec:
  global:
    moduleConfig:
      fileFormat: zip
      immutable: true
    storageConfig:
      s3:
        bucket: opendepot-modules
        region: us-east-1
  moduleConfigs:
    - name: terraform-aws-vpc
      provider: aws
      repoOwner: terraform-aws-modules
      versionConstraints: ">= 5.0.0"
    - name: terraform-aws-eks
      provider: aws
      repoOwner: terraform-aws-modules
      versionConstraints: ">= 20.0.0, != 21.13.0"
    - name: terraform-google-kubernetes-engine
      provider: google
      repoOwner: terraform-google-modules
      versionConstraints: ">= 33.0.0"
  pollingIntervalMinutes: 360

The Depot queries each repository's GitHub releases, filters them by constraint, creates Module and Version resources, and stores the archives. When module IaC scanning is enabled, the Version controller runs trivy fs with the misconfig scanner on each archive. This flags HCL issues such as open security groups, public S3 ACLs, or unencrypted storage.

Note

Module IaC scanning does not use the Trivy vulnerability database. To run it without the database PVC, CronJob, and cache volume, disable provider scanning: 

scanning:
  enabled: true
  providerScanning: false
See Vulnerability Scanning for the full configuration reference.

With pollingIntervalMinutes: 360, the Depot checks for new releases every six hours.

docs.title: Combined example
docs.text:
A single Depot can manage modules and providers together:

apiVersion: opendepot.defdev.io/v1alpha1
kind: Depot
metadata:
  name: my-team-depot
  namespace: opendepot-system
spec:
  global:
    githubClientConfig:
      useAuthenticatedClient: true
    moduleConfig:
      fileFormat: zip
      immutable: true
    storageConfig:
      s3:
        bucket: opendepot-modules
        region: us-west-2
  moduleConfigs:
    - name: terraform-aws-eks
      provider: aws
      repoOwner: terraform-aws-modules
      versionConstraints: ">= 21.10.1, != 21.13.0"
    - name: terraform-azurerm-aks
      provider: azurerm
      repoOwner: azure
      versionConstraints: ">= 10.0.0"
  providerConfigs:
    - name: aws
      operatingSystems:
        - linux
      architectures:
        - amd64
        - arm64
      versionConstraints: ">= 5.80.0"
      storageConfig:
        s3:
          bucket: opendepot-modules
          region: us-west-2
  pollingIntervalMinutes: 60

This Depot:

  1. Queries the terraform-aws-modules/terraform-aws-eks and azure/terraform-azurerm-aks repositories for releases that match the constraints, and creates Module resources
  2. Queries the upstream registry for aws and creates a Provider resource
  3. Has the Module and Provider controllers create Version resources, which the Version controller fetches and stores
  4. Re-checks for new releases every 60 minutes

docs.title: Branch sources
docs.text:
